title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
City of Edmonton
Closing Date: October 19, 2026, 11:59 PM (MDT)
This is your chance to join Canada’s top public sector data science program!
Collaborating with teams across the Corporation, Senior Data Scientists bridge the divide between raw data and action, with an emphasis on solving real world problems and operationalizing solutions.
The Senior Data Scientist position is dedicated to leading and shaping end-to-end data science projects. This role serves as the driving force behind data science at the City of Edmonton and the application of insights to fulfill organizational objectives.

title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
What You Will Do

Project Intake: Decide on whether a project requires data science approaches such as machine learning, clustering, and forecasting. Do research on potential solutions, and project directions.
Project Leadership: Lead and manage complex data science projects, aligning them with corporate objectives and incorporating project planning, scheduling, resourcing, risk assessment, and cost/benefit analyses. Guide junior staff and mentor data science students on projects, and coordinate efforts between those involved.
Data Analysis: Analyze large and intricate datasets to extract meaningful insights that drive strategic decisions, considering the size, scope, duration, risk, and complexity of the projects.
Model Development: Develop and implement advanced predictive models and algorithms to address business challenges, leveraging specialized systems and technology (e.g., Unix, Docker, Databases, Scripting) for production-level implementation.
Operationalization: Work with Community partners to design a solution that can be used by front-line staff, and monitor usage as a key metric of project success.
Quality Assurance: Rigorously test and validate data-driven solutions to ensure accuracy, reliability, and alignment with the organization’s strategic direction.
Performance Monitoring: Continuously monitor the performance of deployed models, adapting and interpreting them as necessary to reduce uncertainty and increase the likelihood of success. Collaborate with the Data and Analytics Ethicist to examine ethical implications. This includes preparing progress reports and escalating project concerns to project governance.
Model Optimization: Iteratively improve machine learning models as needed to enhance predictive accuracy and relevance to business goals.
Stakeholder Communication: Effectively communicate complex findings and insights to non-technical Community Partners, including senior management, to influence the Corporation’s strategic direction.
Continual Learning: Stay up to date with new advancements in the field of data science broadly, with a specific emphasis on learning innovative techniques directly beneficial to the end-to-end implementation of data science projects at the City.
Perform other related duties.

title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
Qualifications

Graduate University Degree in applied statistics, mathematics, engineering, computer science, or a related field.
8 years experience with an emphasis on complex operationalized artificial intelligence projects.
Project Management Professional (PMP) Designation is required. Applicants who currently do not possess their PMP Designation may be considered and if successful, will be required to obtain it within the first 12 months of employment.

title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
Skills Required for Success

Proficient in multivariate regression/classification, time series models, cluster analysis, anomaly detection, optimization, neural network models, supervised and unsupervised machine learning techniques.
Experience using state of the art machine-learning techniques (e.g., BERT, YOLO, XGBoost).
Proficiency in relational databases, SQL, and scripting languages (e.g., R, Python).
Experience with Generative AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks and architectures.
Experience with agent development frameworks such as Google ADK (or equivalents like LangGraph or LlamaIndex) and self-hosted model inference such as Ollama or vLLM.
Strong programming skills with experience in software development in a collaborative environment.
Demonstrated success in applying machine learning and statistical methods to solve practical problems.
Inherently motivated, intellectually curious, and inclined towards taking proactive actions.
Strong critical thinking, consensus-building, and influential skills.
Self-directed and capable of managing complex projects independently.
Proficient in project management with a track record of implementing improvements at organizational, departmental, and operational levels.
Effective communication skills tailored for diverse audiences, proven through successful information dissemination and active listening.
Alignment to our Cultural Commitments and Leadership Competencies.
Embracing a culture of equity, diversity, reconciliation and inclusion.
Applicants may be tested.

title: Projects
text: Here is the work behind my Skills response. Public examples come first. Internal projects document my contribution, but their code, data, and reports are not publicly accessible. These are research and Alberta public-service examples, not previous City of Edmonton work.

title: Projects
text:
Public Work

E01 — Caseload Forecast Demo
I built an R forecasting demonstration using 246 months of Alberta Income Support open data. Seasonal ARIMA is compared with a seasonal-naive baseline over a 24-month holdout; forecasts include 80% and 95% prediction intervals and traceable training inputs. This deliberately simplified example of the internal forecasting pipeline provides a concrete basis for planning cloud deployment.
Local learning demonstration, not a production or cloud deployment. Forecasts reflect the example’s data snapshot, not a current operational forecast.
Forecast site · Repository


E02 — Absent From Chronic
This is a full-cycle demonstration of agentic analytics. I developed reproducible workflows for a collaborative study of chronic conditions and work absenteeism using 63,843 employed Canadian Community Health Survey respondents. Variable definitions, data validation, missingness and outcome diagnostics, and LASSO selection connect the research question to the analysis.
This project exemplifies my current approach to human-AI collaboration across engineering, modelling, and publishing processes.
Analysis site · Repository · Project overview


E05 — Quick-Start Template And Agent Harness
I adapted and extended Will Beasley’s RAnalysisSkeleton for GoA research. The shared project framework became the basis for 32 branch repositories, with conventions for data preparation, version control, and documentation.
Since 2023, I’ve maintained the template and expanded it from prompt customization into an agent harness for data engineering, modelling, and frontend publishing. The adoption count describes the project framework, not deployment of every later AI feature.
Template · AI support system · Design principles · Minding the Agents · AI for Data Science Teams

title: Projects
text:
Internal Applied Work

E03 — FIESTA
I initiated and led the Financial Impact of Employment Services and Training in Alberta (FIESTA) project to produce defensible estimates of the impact of provincial employment services. My contribution included study design, cohort assembly, record linkage and assessment of linkage bias, propensity-score weighting, estimation, and reporting. Findings informed provincial employment-service funding decisions and laid the foundation for annual impact-assessment reporting.
Completed evaluation and stakeholder reporting. The repository, technical report, and methodological presentations are internal GoA resources.


E04 — FIESTA 2.0
The 2023 FIESTA evaluation attracted further interest from leadership. To support annual reporting using data linked to tax records, I built a versioned, three-stage preparation pipeline covering 734,000 individuals and more than 8.6 million records. The data were prepared for transfer to Alberta’s Office of Statistical Information for the next, more expansive round of analysis. I provided analysis-ready data, reproducibility documentation, and methodological advice.
Preparation pipeline implemented. This is distinct from the original evaluation and its findings; the repository is internal.


E06 — Research Database
My first GoA project aimed to help my unit move from a SAS-and-Excel workflow to reproducible R/SQL workflows. I introduced a research data-warehousing practice and developed R/SQL Server research infrastructure integrating more than 15 administrative source tables. Consultation with business-intelligence and modelling colleagues shaped the design. Documented transformations support recurring reports, information requests, and a variety of analytical notebooks.
Established research/reporting infrastructure. Repository and administrative data are internal.


E07 — Employability-Readiness Reporting
More than 3,000 Albertans complete the Employability Readiness Assessment (ERA) each month to help connect them with provincial employment services and training. I modernized and integrated reporting scripts into a documented, reproducible framework. It supports weekly processing and reports every two weeks for employment-service staff.
Recurring operational reporting. Repository and administrative data are internal.


E08 — Work Outcomes Reporting Project (WORP)
I work with the survey manager and lead statistician on monthly survey-reporting modernization. My contribution is reproducible architecture, templatization, automation, and AI-assisted development in workflows involving response verification, nonresponse weighting, and reporting alerts.
Collaborative modernization of an existing process. Repository internal; the statistical and operational work has shared ownership.


E13 — Open-Data Report Preparation
Assisted Living and Social Services has a mandate to publish its key indicators. I collaborated on automating Income Support caseload report preparation from artifacts approved for release. Scripted analysis, visualization, and report generation replace manual preparation. For a public example, see the June 2026 Income Support report (PDF). The Caseload Forecast Demo uses Income Support open data to illustrate forecasting pipelines.
Automated preparation, not release approval. The repository remains internal despite its open-data subject.

title: Projects
text:
Teaching And Learning

E09 — VADA Summer School
I served on the advisory committee of the Visual and Automated Disease Analytics (VADA) graduate training program and delivered multiple training sessions and demonstrations at its events. See my VADA profile and June 2019 workshop materials on reproducible visualization in R and GitHub for data science. The workshops connect version control, project organization, and visual explanation through working examples.


E10 — Thinking Together, Working Apart
During my Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) fellowship, I co-authored Thinking Together, Working Apart and served as the project’s analytical lead. The article examines communities of practice for productive, meaningful remote collaboration. It was published online in 2020 and appeared in the September 2021 issue.


E11 — Knowledge Onboarding And Colleague Support
I thrive in collaborative learning. Most of my career has involved developing curricula and designing learning experiences. After joining GoA, I initiated a structured capacity-building effort. I delivered more than 15 sessions on analytical tools, data, and reproducible workflows, and helped more than a dozen colleagues establish GitHub, VS Code, and Copilot workflows. Recordings, transcripts, and edited materials from our year-long learning series formed the foundation of an onboarding guide for new analysts in my unit.
The onboarding guide and recordings are internal. The VADA workshop materials provide a public example of my teaching.


E12 — Practitioner Participation And AI Learning
I participate in GoA Copilot learning sessions, the Data Analyst Network, and Alberta AI Academy activities. My AIM sandbox is a public example created to support the Academy’s curriculum.

title: Responsibilities
text:
Frame the question. I start with the decision someone needs to make, then work back to the evidence. In FIESTA, that meant studying employment-service outcomes, examining bias, and reporting findings that informed funding decisions. A useful answer matters more than an elaborate model.
Build something inspectable. Much of my work sits between a good question and data that can answer it. I’ve built research infrastructure and large preparation pipelines, with documented transformations that colleagues can follow and reuse. That foundation matters whichever modelling stack comes next.
Make it useful. Delivery means more than finishing the analysis. My employment-readiness work supports recurring reports for service staff; survey modernization is shared work with the people who know the process. I’d bring that same attention to how a City team would actually use a solution.
Lead and keep learning. I can lead a study and still need other people’s expertise. I help colleagues build their workflows and develop shared tools, including an agent harness. When a project calls for a different stack, I’d learn it through a small working example, with the team’s expectations for testing and support built in.
The project responsibilities as you describe them overlap with how I think about them, in three phases: frame, build, and deliver.

title: Responsibilities
text:
Specific Response

Project intake: decide whether data science is needed, research possible solutions, and choose a useful direction.

I’d clarify the decision, the available data, and what a useful result would look like before choosing a method. My forecast demo compares ARIMA with a simple seasonal baseline: extra complexity has to earn its place.

Project leadership: align complex projects with organizational goals; plan time, resources, risks, and costs and benefits; coordinate and mentor others.

I led FIESTA from design to reporting and help colleagues develop their tools and workflows. For a City project, I’d agree on milestones, ownership, capacity, risks, and the expected benefit early, then make trade-offs visible as the work develops.

Data analysis: turn large, complex datasets into useful evidence, with the project’s scale, duration, and risks in view.

This is familiar ground. FIESTA brought linkage, weighting, estimation, and bias assessment together around a service question. For FIESTA 2.0, I built the preparation pipeline for more than 8.6 million records; the Office of Statistical Information leads linkage and estimation for that phase.

Model development: build predictive solutions to business problems and implement them using production technologies such as Unix, Docker, databases, and scripting.

My forecasting comparison and LASSO work show model development, not production ML deployment. R, SQL, and reproducible pipelines give me a base to build on. I’d learn the team’s deployment stack by taking a small model through its testing, packaging, and handoff process.

Operationalization: work with service partners on a solution front-line staff can use, and track whether they use it.

The closest example is employment-readiness reporting: I integrated colleagues’ scripts into a repeatable workflow for service staff. I’d work with users on the format and timing, then agree on a usage measure. Recurring delivery is a starting point, not proof of adoption.

Quality assurance: test accuracy and reliability, and check that the solution still serves the organization’s purpose.

I make the checks part of the analysis: linkage bias in FIESTA, missingness and outcome diagnostics, and holdout validation for forecasting. I’d agree on acceptance criteria with the service team so a technically sound result also answers the right question.

Performance monitoring: track and adapt deployed models, examine ethical implications with the Data and Analytics Ethicist, report progress, and escalate concerns.

My survey-reporting work involves verification and reporting alerts, rather than ownership of a deployed-model monitoring system. I’d build from that: agree on performance measures, review intervals, and escalation thresholds; work with the ethicist on uneven effects; and make concerns visible in progress reports.

Model optimization: improve predictive performance as needed while keeping the business goal in view.

I’d check that a change improves the decision, not just a score. The forecast demo shows baseline comparison and prediction intervals, not a live tuning programme. For an operational model, I’d use agreed validation data and weigh any gain against added complexity and maintenance.

Stakeholder communication: explain findings to non-technical partners and senior management so they can act on them.

I’d lead with what the finding changes, how certain it is, and what it doesn’t tell us, with technical detail available behind it. FIESTA’s findings informed funding decisions; my visualization workshops show another way I help people work with evidence.

Continual learning: learn new methods that help deliver useful data-science projects at the City.

I’ve been extending a shared research template into an agent harness, alongside practitioner learning. I want new tools to solve a real problem; a different stack is something to learn for the work, not a reason to force the work into a familiar tool.

Other related duties: contribute to the surrounding work that keeps projects useful.

Documentation, shared tools, and helping colleagues get started are part of delivery too. My onboarding work is one example; I’d make room for that work in the project plan.

title: Skills
text:
Engineering. R is my home language; SQL and relational data are daily work. I build research infrastructure and repeatable reports, not just one-off analyses. I’m familiar with Python, but wouldn’t claim the same depth. I am a scientist first and a software engineer second.
AI in my own work. I use it to help engineer data, explore it, and publish the results. My agent harness organizes that collaboration; Absent from Chronic shows it at work. The question for me is how to make an analyst’s work more useful and inspectable, not simply generate more code.
Methods. I am a methodologist by training. My PhD in quantitative methods prepared me to learn, adapt, and evaluate methods as the question requires. I connect substantive theory, research design, and modelling in employment-service evaluation, forecasting comparisons, and population research. The aim is a credible answer, with a clear distinction between prediction, explanation, and the effects of an intervention.
Working together. I can carry a study from question to report, but independent work needn’t be solitary. I build with colleagues, teach and mentor, and make tools others can reuse. Listening to the people who know the service matters as much as explaining the model. Shared examples give us something concrete to discuss, question, and improve.
Room to grow. I am building my career toward more advanced applications of statistical learning and data science. That’s a central reason I’m applying to your team. I would bring a strong foundation in statistical modelling, data engineering, and research design, while learning from colleagues whose expertise complements mine. I want to contribute to useful work from the outset and become a stronger data scientist and software engineer through the work we do together.
Public service. Your commitments fit how I want to work: be helpful, accountable, and willing to learn. For equity, diversity, reconciliation, and inclusion, I’d start by listening, questioning whose experience the data misses, and learning from colleagues and communities rather than assuming expertise.

title: Skills
text:
Specific Response

Breadth across regression, time series, clustering, anomaly detection, optimization, neural networks, and supervised and unsupervised methods.

I am a methodologist by training. My doctoral work in quantitative methods gave me a broad foundation in statistical learning and applied research in the social sciences. It prepared me to learn and critically evaluate unfamiliar methods, adapt established approaches, and develop and validate a tailored approach when existing methods do not adequately address the problem.
Over the past decade, much of my applied work has involved generalized linear models, multilevel and mixture modelling, longitudinal analysis, and structural equation modelling. I have also worked with principal component analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and multidimensional scaling to investigate structure in multivariate data. These are the methods my research questions have most often called for, rather than the boundaries of my practice. I choose methods around the question, the data structure, and the assumptions needed to support a credible answer.

Hands-on use of current machine-learning techniques (e.g. BERT, YOLO, XGBoost).

Most of my work concerns structured, rectangular data and questions about people, services, and outcomes. I use methods such as XGBoost when the problem calls for them. I have also explored natural-language methods, including MPNet—enough to build on when needed, though I would not claim specialist expertise.
My deeper experience is in connecting substantive theory, research design, and statistical modelling. In much of my work, the greatest gains come from clarifying the question, improving measurement, and establishing credible comparisons—not simply improving predictive fit. I value flexible predictive models, while distinguishing what helps predict an outcome from what supports an explanation or a decision about intervention.

Relational databases, SQL, and scripting in R or Python.

This is a clear fit: R is my home language, SQL and relational data are daily work, and Python is familiar. The research database and repeatable reporting show that work in practice.

Generative AI and retrieval-augmented systems.

I use generative AI in analytical workflows, but that isn’t production RAG experience. My agent harness and Absent from Chronic show what I’ve built so far.

Agent-development frameworks and self-hosted model inference.

I’ve developed an agent harness, not deployed the specific frameworks or self-hosted inference systems named. I can learn the stack against a bounded, testable task. See the agent harness.

Collaborative software development and strong programming.

My software work is collaborative and analytical: shared templates, pipelines, and reporting tools. The quick-start template and survey-reporting modernization show the pattern. For a longer view of my work, explore my GitHub contributions, which date back to 2012.

Applying statistical and machine-learning methods to practical problems.

Sums up what I do in practice. See examples: FIESTA, the forecast demo, and Absent from Chronic.

Initiative, curiosity, and proactive learning.

Learning is what I do; that’s my primary job security.

Critical thinking, consensus-building, and influence.

My professional motto is “knowledge is a conversation,” a theme of my AI for Data Science Teams talk. Objective truth does not depend on agreement, but scientific claims must be supported by evidence and exposed to criticism. Peer review and open discussion do not make a claim true; they help us uncover errors, challenge assumptions, and distinguish persuasive arguments from reliable findings. For me, convincing others means making my reasoning available for inspection, answering objections, and being willing to revise my conclusions. Without that exchange, confidence can outpace the evidence.
I test assumptions, examine bias, and work through design with colleagues. The FIESTA evaluation and research database are good examples.

Independent delivery of complex projects.

I can carry a study from design through reporting. The original FIESTA evaluation is the clearest example; the research database shows longer-running infrastructure work.

Project management and improvements across organizational, departmental, and operational settings.

I’ve led evaluation work and built repeatable reporting infrastructure. Those examples show practical delivery, not a claim to have worked at every scale described: FIESTA, the research database, and employment-readiness reporting.

Communication for different audiences, including clear information-sharing and active listening.

I turn technical work into reports, help colleagues learn, and listen to service experts as part of the analysis. See employment-readiness reporting, colleague support, and survey modernization.

Alignment with the City’s cultural commitments and leadership expectations.

I want to work in a way that’s useful, accountable, and open to learning. Your commitments fit that, and how I work with colleagues is one example.

Equity, diversity, reconciliation, and inclusion.

I’d start by listening, asking whose experience the data may miss, and learning with colleagues and communities rather than claiming expertise I don’t have. FIESTA and survey modernization offer examples of applied work with service and survey contexts.

Openness to an assessment of skills.

I’m comfortable showing my work; the forecast demo and Absent from Chronic are concrete places to start a technical discussion.

title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
Do you practice what you preach? How is AI injected into your own work? Into your pipelines for extracting and engineering data, into scripts for exploration and visualization, modeling and interpretation? How do you constrain AI agents when you compose literate scripts of analytic reports that uncover and document the evidence found in your data?
If you are looking for ways to elevate the work of your data scientists through the integration of AI into advanced analytic practices, my work and experience might be relevant to your vision of growth.
There are many ways into Data Science. I came from statistics for social sciences, picking up tech along the way. From psych to health, I framed my work around studying populations, understanding groups of people using the data they generate. I still think in this way. After I started with the Government of Alberta in 2021, I built practices for research data warehousing and reproducible reporting to support the study of social programs and their recipients. But around 2025 I stopped perceiving my role as the writer of code, instead, I began seeing myself as the orchestrator of processes. In my flavour of data science, the big three are: engineering, visualizing, and publishing.
The template for reproducible research projects I developed and maintained for GoA since 2023 was expanded to include tools for context engineering and agent specialization. I started with a simple AI Support System that steered the agent via streamlined customization of the system prompt. Over time it evolved into a more intentional and specific agent harness for scientific reporting that organized human-AI collaboration in three key processes of data science: data engineering, modeling, and frontend publishing. To get a better feel for how it works and what it makes, consider my Absent from Chronic project.
Substantively, it seeks to understand the role of chronic conditions in work absenteeism using the data from the Canadian Community Health Survey (AfC project overview). Technically, I aimed to demonstrate the utility of my AI harness in solving practical problems in applied analytics. You can examine the codebase in this repo, while my recent talks offer a high-level summary of the harness design (Minding the Agents) and a few thoughts on collaboration in data science (AI for Data Science Teams), both featuring this reproducible project.
Why your team. AI is not a magic bullet, it needs well-defined problems and willing stakeholders to bring about operational impact. Your internal consultancy gets it and puts it into practice. I want to measure my career by making cool things that benefit people: the Corporation lacks neither diversity nor volume of problems to tackle and your team seems to be having fun solving them. I will be delighted to explore how our partnership can benefit the people who call Edmonton home.

title: Qualifications
text:
Education. PhD in Quantitative Methods (2014), MA in Quantitative Psychology (2008), and BS in Journalism (2005). More in my CV.
Experience. Over the past ten years, my work has combined applied statistics, research, and data science: IALSA research at the University of Victoria, a CIHR Health System Impact Fellowship at UBC, clinical research at Island Health, and an assistant professorship in Health Management and Informatics at the University of Central Florida. For the past five years, I’ve worked with the Government of Alberta on service impact evaluation and research data infrastructure. During the last year I explored modernizing our forecasting capacities in preparation for cloud deployment. My agent-assisted project template provides the blueprint for any recent analytical work.
PMP. I took project-management training during my CIHR fellowship and am ready and willing to obtain the PMP designation within the first 12 months. I don’t currently hold the designation; my project leadership experience gives me a practical foundation for the formal certification.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Research checked: October 8, 2026
Scope: Publicly available resources located online about the City of Edmonton’s Data Science and Research (DSR) team, publicly named members and collaborators, named projects, and the municipal context in which the team works. This is a source-based profile, not a complete staff directory or internal project register.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Overview
The City describes DSR as a team applying data science and artificial intelligence (AI) to operational municipal problems. Its public examples emphasize working with service-area staff and subject-matter experts, selecting methods that fit the decision, and planning for operational use rather than treating a model as a stand-alone research result. A 2025 presentation describes the group as a centralized team formed in 2020; a City article about WildEdmonton says it was founded in 2021. The sources may be describing different milestones, so the exact founding date is unclear.
The City article describes the team as having eight members at the time it was written, but it does not name them all. The 2025 Upper Bound session identifies four team presenters. Those four are the publicly named members that can be confidently associated with the team from the sources found here; this should not be read as a complete or current roster. A 2018 City data-science event identifies earlier contributors, shown separately below.
In September 2026, Taproot reported that the applied AI division had completed 77 projects and had 50 at different stages in its queue. Public coverage therefore documents only a fraction of the team’s work; the project list below is limited to initiatives for which a public source was found.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Publicly Documented Projects
Names, status, and level of attribution below follow the linked sources. “Current” indicates described as active or operational in the cited material, not independently verified as of the research date.



Project
Purpose and public status
People or partners linked in sources




Ember Wise / Amberwise
Wildfire-risk monitoring and forecasting. The Upper Bound presentation describes use of weather, forest-fuel, and topographic information; a location-based risk component is operational, while use of calls-for-service data to explore behavior-related ignition risk was still in development. Amii’s session description spells the name “Amberwise”; the presentation notes use “Ember Wise.”
Zehra Shah presented this work.


Residential safety-code inspection triage
A model to help prioritize discretionary residential safety-code inspections. The 2025 talk stresses that mandatory inspections remain required and describes choosing error thresholds with inspectors and operational partners. Earlier City and award coverage describes the Safety Codes Inspection Efficiencies (SCIE) initiative; public sources do not establish that every historical and current model version is identical.
Clayton Clemens presented the 2025 project. Ben Gready is associated with the earlier SCIE initiative.


Repair
A map-based workflow for filtering and prioritizing pothole reports, with historical information and next-week pothole estimates by road zone. The Upper Bound talk says the team moved from trying to predict individual notifications to forecasting counts by zone because report descriptions and images were often missing. A voice-activated reporting app was shown as a prototype.
Taher Abbasi presented the project.


WildEdmonton
City–University of Alberta wildlife monitoring partnership, running since 2018. The City’s account says the DSR team built an AI-assisted image workflow using Microsoft’s CameraTraps MegaDetector to identify and filter images containing people, improving privacy and processing efficiency for wildlife research.
City of Edmonton, University of Alberta, and DSR; the City identifies Clayton Clemens as a Senior Data Scientist involved in the work.


Unison
Public-safety data and deployment tool that combines partner incident-demand information into a shared operating picture. Reporting describes Decide for forecasting areas of demand and Track for monitoring trends and interventions. Its stated approach includes data minimization and excluding sensitive attributes and crime data that could produce feedback loops.
Kris Andreychuk is identified as an architect of the tool. Reporting names City and community partners.


Text Depot
Internal search and analysis tool for municipal text records. The City of Edmonton GitHub repository describes a dashboard for searching and analyzing text stored in Elasticsearch. An Apolitical case study attributes the broader platform to DSR and describes its internal use.
Attributed to the DSR team in the case study; the City maintains a public GitHub repository for the dashboard.


Exposure
Earlier project that scraped online “body rub” listings to help outreach workers identify people who might need assistance. Andreychuk said the project was taken over by police and later ended after the source site shut down.
Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting; not a current DSR project.


Symbol Smart
Image-detection application intended to identify hate symbols. Andreychuk described the project as stalling because the departments that could use it could not agree on ownership.
Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting; status described as unsuccessful/stalled.


Used-needle collection route optimization
Route-optimization work for pickups from public bins. Andreychuk described learning that operational staff did not find the proposed routes useful; the public account does not document its eventual disposition.
Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting.


Workforce-injury reduction
A project described as upcoming in September 2026 reporting; no public project name, technical details, or assigned team members were provided in the source.
No individuals identified in the source.



The City and partner sources also refer to broader AI and data-science work, but do not publish a complete list of the 77 reported completed projects or the 50 queued projects. The items above are the named initiatives substantiated in the sources collected here, not an exhaustive portfolio.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Source Notes And Limitations

The 2025 Amii session names four presenters; the City-published WildEdmonton article says the team had eight members but does not name the other four. Neither source establishes the full present-day staffing roster.
Public accounts differ on whether the team was formed in 2020 or founded in 2021. Both claims are retained here rather than selecting one without evidence.
The wildfire project name appears as “Ember Wise” in the presentation materials and “Amberwise” in Amii’s session summary.
Project names, operating status, and member associations are limited to what the cited public sources state. Similar project labels do not by themselves prove that models described in different years are the same implementation.
Some project descriptions rely on reporting and partner case studies rather than a City project page. Links are included so readers can distinguish those accounts from City-published resources.
